Vuelta a España 2026: Our GC form guide

With the Giro d’Italia and Tour de France crossed off our list, one Grand Tour remains in 2026: the Vuelta a España.

The Spanish Grand Tour will start outside of Spain this year, with an opening time-trial taking place in Monaco on Saturday before the race makes its way west through France towards its home nation over the next few days. However, Slovenia will likely be the nation in the spotlight on the start line thanks to Tadej Pogačar deciding to make his Vuelta return seven years after his only previous appearance at the race. Safe to say he’s the runaway favourite, but If anything goes topsy-turvy for the five-time Tour champion, Richard Carapaz, João Almeida, Oscar Onley and Felix Gall will be on hand to profit.

For those looking to weigh up the options for your fantasy team or place a sneaky bet, we’ve got you covered here. We’ll go through the 15 leading favourites for the 2026 Vuelta a España – according to the betting odds – taking you through their recent performances to bring you a horse racing-style form guide.

Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

When Tadej Pogačar announced his Vuelta participation in early August, the reaction was unanimous. Our winner had already been decided.

This consensus is founded on some reasonable thinking. Pogačar has won on more than half of his race days this year and he’s only missed one big objective for the year: Paris-Roubaix. He’s won every stage race he’s entered since 2023, and across his career he’s won more Grand Tours than he’s lost – six versus three.

Everything points toward a Pogačar victory. You could even say this has the potential to be the most one-sided Grand Tour of modern times.

Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost)

Richard Carapaz made the decision to come to the Vuelta at the last minute. However, judging from recent form, this was likely a smart idea.

The Ecuadorian has been on a streak of good form lately in one-day races and stage races. This started with a runner-up spot at the Tour de Suisse before an aggressive Tour de France that resulted in two stage wins and a top ten on GC. Most recently, he was pipped by Remco Evenepoel to the Klasikoa title, but the EF rider left a strong impression on the climbs.

Carapaz is a consistent GC rider when he decides to lock in from day one. Almost half of his Grand Tour starts since 2019 have resulted in a podium, so he’s got pedigree in a three-week race. What’s more, he is said to be looking for a new contract.

Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM)

Felix Gall has been one of the most consistent stage racers this year. Of course, his Giro podium demonstrated that, but the Austrian hasn’t finished outside the top six of a stage race all year.

His climbing is his greatest asset. On the Vuelta’s numerous mountaintop finishes, the Austrian should have what it takes to hang on with the strongest attacks. He proved that at the Giro, although I suspect the climbing field here is on a higher level. If that’s a worry though, Gall defeated a whole host of the big Vuelta names recently at the Vuelta a Burgos.

João Almeida (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

At the beginning of the season, João Almeida was expected to be UAE Team Emirates XRG’s leader for the Vuelta. Nine months on, teammate Pogačar is on the start line and Almeida has had to completely reorganise his season after a succession of illnesses and injuries.

The Portuguese rider was forced to skip several WorldTour races in the spring, including a leadership position at the Giro d’Italia. The summer was then filled with DNFs at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and the Tour de Pologne. That leaves Almeida with just one WorldTour result on his 2026 record: a 38th place at the Volta a Catalunya.

If he’s recovered from a crash at the Tour de Pologne, Almeida has the pedigree to reach the podium. On the other hand, his results have been meagre this year and his team’s priorities will be focused on Pogačar.

Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos)

After a series of setbacks in 2026, Oscar Onley looks set to start his first Grand Tour in Netcompany Ineos colours, his first since that breakthrough Tour de France performance in 2025.

Onley has pulled out of several key races this year as a result of crashes and injury. His most serious incident was back at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, where he dislocated his shoulder midway through a stage. The Scot has recovered, however, and looked to be in good shape at the Vuelta a Burgos, where he finished second overall after a stage victory.

His climbing legs are up to scratch and his punch appears to be more explosive than it was in 2025. That should place him in good stead to chase the podium and the white jersey, a prize Ineos have never won at the Vuelta a España.

Enric Mas (Movistar)

Spain’s best chance of a podium seems to be Enric Mas, who starts as one of the bookies’ third tier of favourites for victory (albeit at a distant 20-1 odds). Most of this stems from Mas’s Vuelta record of three second places and a third in the final GC.

This season, however, Mas has looked under par. He’s failed to make an impact in any WorldTour race, and his Giro d’Italia debut led to a hugely underwhelming 32nd place overall. Fifth at the Vuelta a Burgos earlier this month is slightly less disappointing, but Mas always seems to find a way to pull a decent GC result at the Vuelta.

Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe)

Roglič has an impressive record at the Vuelta. He’s started the race on six occasions and won a total of four times. In fact, the only time the Slovenian hasn’t ended up on the podium, he quit the race midway through. Like his countryman Pogačar managed at the Tour earlier this year though, Roglič has the chance to make it five wins overall at this year’s Vuelta, which would make him the race’s most successful rider in history.

The four-time champion is somewhat past his prime, however. This year, he’s only managed to finish inside the top ten of a stage race once, while appearances at the Tour de Suisse and Tour de Romandie had little impact. His one-day record has also been subpar, but you can never count Roglič out at a Vuelta.

Mattias Skjelmose (Lidl-Trek)

Mattias Skjelmose rode his debut Vuelta in 2024. Then, he finished a solid fifth place overall and won the white jersey in Madrid. This time aged 25, he doesn’t have the white jersey to aim for, just ambitions of reaching the podium.

In 2026, the Dane has been incredibly consistent in both the Classics and stage races. Last month, Skjelmose rode a steady Tour de France to finish sixth overall, the same position he managed at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and one ahead of his placement at the Volta a Catalunya. Unlike at the Tour, he won’t need to share leadership duties with Juan Ayuso and will enter the Vuelta as the team’s outright leader.

Tobias Halland Johannessen (Uno-X Mobility)

After a late-minute change of heart, it looks as though Tobias Halland Johannessen will lead Uno-X Mobility at the Vuelta.

The Norwegian has been in solid form all year, particularly in stage races. Johannessen finished 3rd, 4th and 5th at top-flight WorldTour races ahead of a Tour bid that was more angled towards the breakaway than a top ten overall. Having finished sixth at the 2025 Tour, this year’s result felt disappointing, so the hope of a strong GC result could have motivated his late Vuelta start.

This will be the Norwegian’s Vuelta debut. However, Uno-X are in the midst of a phenomenal year, from Fredrik Dversnes’s Giro stage win to Torstein Træen and Sigrid Haugset’s stints in yellow at the Tour de France. It would be surprising to see the team underperform here in Spain.

Jørgen Nordhagen (Visma-Lease a Bike)

It’s a bit surprising to see Jørgen Nordhagen inside the bookies’ top ten.

The Norwegian is seen as the long-term heir to Jonas Vingegaard’s position as team leader, given his strong results at the under-23 level. Nordhagen is still just 21, but his first full season on the WorldTour has been impressive. A top ten at the UAE Tour was a good sign, but a fourth at the Tour de Romandie was more convincing.

Nordhagen’s recent performance at the Vuelta a Burgos, on the other hand, drew some concern. A 27th place overall there doesn’t necessarily suggest that he’s set for a Seixas-like Grand Tour debut.

Matthew Riccitello (Decathlon CMA CGM)

Matthew Riccitello was one of the top performers at last year’s Vuelta, when the Arizonan reached Madrid in fifth place.

He’s since moved teams and found some success at Decathlon CMA CGM. His three wins this season came earlier in the season before he swapped out his own ambitions in order to support teammate Paul Seixas at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and Tour de France.

At the Vuelta, Riccitello will be a domestique again, this time for Felix Gall. A top ten is possible, but it won’t be Riccitello’s priority.

Cian Uijtdebroeks (Movistar)

Cian Uijtdebroeks is another rider who has yet to fully deliver despite having been touted for big things. After several team transfers, he’s hoping his new Spanish team Movistar will provide the missing link for him to reach his Grand Tour potential.

The Belgian’s form this year has been mixed. He had to abandon the Tour de France, but did manage to claim a couple of top tens at stage races earlier in the season. On the whole, nothing quite stands out, which is largely a continuation of the B-tier status Uijtdebroeks has struggled to break clear of throughout his career to date.

The Belgian’s Grand Tour record is filled with DNFs. Still, if he manages to reach the end of the Vuelta – something he’s not done in three years – he will likely be on the fringes of the top ten.

Jay Vine (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

Jay Vine is the third UAE rider to feature on this list. However, I suggest he’s the least likely to reach the podium, given he’s never targeted it before.

Regardless, Vine has a good relationship with the Vuelta, having won four stages and two polka-dot jerseys at the Spanish race. Vine is a bit clumsy though. He’s abandoned half the Grand Tours he’s entered and most of his race appearances this year have also ended with a towel being thrown in.

If he stays upright, Vine will ikely be in the breakaways hunting stages and mountain points.

Luke Tuckwell (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe)

There’s a fair amount of hype behind Australian youngster Luke Tuckwell, who will be making his Grand Tour debut this week.

Tuckwell, who finished runner-up at the Giro Next Gen in 2025, has had a successful neopro season with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe. In April, the Aussie finished sixth at the Tour de Romandie before an impressive run at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, when he finished second overall after gaining time from a midweek breakaway.

Tuckwell can time-trial well, so he might be in the frame once the race hits the mountains shortly after the prologue. However, his results don’t quite show enough evidence for him to be a legitimate top ten contender.

Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike)

Sepp Kuss is one of only two riders to start the 2026 Vuelta with a previous race win in their palmarès.

The 2023 winner will enter as one of Visma’s most trusted climbers, but a repeat of 2023 is unlikely. Instead, expect to see Kuss targeting stages and mountain points rather than a second Vuelta title.

Kuss has ridden the Giro and Tour already in 2026, making him the only rider to complete the hat-trick of Grand Tour starts in 2026.
